text:
Anupam Bagchi
1w
Robotics and networking are linked together. The issue is latency experienced with transferring motor positons generated by VLA models during inference time to the actual motors. For development purposes, you may resort to the good old ROS2 middleware which is very powerful but it also comes with massive friction: painful installations, complex DDS networking, bulky Docker containers, and endless dependency hell. 
As robots start having degrees-of-freedom amounting to 100, you will have huge latency issues in production using ROS2. I have seen solutions to this using triple-buffered shared memory - but you need to be a C++ expert to handle this.
On this issue there is a zero-overhead network protocol offered by https://zenoh.io/. This has been used to create a lightweight framework called BabyROS (https://lnkd.in/gHmaY5Wt) which I found quite interesting. According to their site, it solves the following problems:
It strips away the infrastructure bloat of ROS2 so you can focus entirely on building your robot.
Instant Setup: Forget complex system-wide dependencies and workspace sourcing. BabyROS installs via pip and runs entirely on Python + Zenoh.
Simplified Networking: Replaces heavy DDS configuration with Zenoh, delivering native shared memory, ultra-low latency, and seamless cloud-to-edge communication out of the box.
Zero Message Overhead: No more writing .msg boilerplate for every data type. It dynamically serializes Python objects for rapid prototyping and faster experimentation.
Lightweight & Container-Ready: Eliminates massive system-wide libraries, resulting in smaller Docker images, faster CI/CD pipelines, and bulletproof reproducibility.
By moving from local-network-centric, heavy framework constraints to a lightweight, cloud-ready architecture, BabyROS cuts down development overhead and accelerates the path from prototype to deployment.

1w  Edited
Most people still think AI = chatbot.
But the real shift happening right now is much bigger.
We've moved from reactive AI to agentic AI — systems that perceive, plan, act, observe, and iterate until a goal is fully complete. No hand-holding. No step-by-step instructions.
The difference in 2026 is that the "sensors" are now web searches, APIs, and file systems. The "actuators" are code execution, email, and database writes. And the "controller" is a large language model reasoning in natural language.
This convergence is why I believe the gap between software agents and embodied robots is closing faster than most people realize.
Key components every agentic system shares with autonomous robotics:
→ Perception layer (context ingestion)
→ Planning and reasoning engine (LLM + ReAct / chain-of-thought)
→ Action execution (tool use)
→ Feedback and correction loop
→ Safety and scope constraints
→ Observability and logging
I wrote a full breakdown of how this works — from first principles to real-world deployments at companies using LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, and MCP.
